subject: Vocabulary
topic: Word Roots — SCRIB/SCRIPT (write): describe, prescribe, manuscript, inscription
description: Latin root SCRIB/SCRIPTUM (to write): describe, prescribe, subscribe, manuscript, inscription, conscript, proscribe, postscript — meaning, usage, fill-in-blank, distinctions.

questions.stem: The Latin root SCRIB/SCRIPT means 'to write.' Which of the following words does NOT contain this root?

options.option_text: Describe, prescribe, subscribe — all contain SCRIB/SCRIPT root
Sculptor — from SCULPERE (to carve), not from SCRIBERE (to write)
Manuscript — MANU (hand) + SCRIPT (written) = handwritten document
Inscription — IN (on) + SCRIPT (written) = writing carved or printed on a surface

questions.explanation: SCRIB/SCRIPT FAMILY: describe (write down details), prescribe (write beforehand = doctor's order), subscribe (write under = agree to), manuscript (hand-written), inscription (written on stone/metal), conscript (write together = draft into military), postscript (written after = P.S.), transcribe (write across = copy), scripture (holy writings). SCULPTOR: from SCULPERE/SCULPTUM (to carve, cut) — no writing connection. EXAM SKILL: don't confuse words that sound similar. 'Sculptor' and 'script' look related but have different Latin roots.

questions.topic: Word Roots — SCRIB/SCRIPT (write): describe, prescribe, manuscript, inscription

questions.stem: A doctor 'prescribes' medicine. The prefix PRE means 'before.' What does prescribe literally convey?

options.option_text: To write before (beforehand) — the doctor writes the order in advance of the patient obtaining medicine
To forbid or ban — that is PROSCRIBE (PRO = in front of/publicly + SCRIBE = write); different prefix
To write one's name under — that is SUBSCRIBE (SUB = under + SCRIBE = write) (not this)
To write again or rewrite — that is TRANSCRIBE or REWRITE, not PRESCRIBE (not this)

questions.explanation: PRESCRIBE: PRE (before) + SCRIBE (write) = write beforehand. MEDICAL USE: doctor writes the prescription (written order) before the pharmacist dispenses. EXTENDED USE: 'prescribed procedure' = specified in advance. PROSCRIBE (CRITICAL DISTINCTION): PRO (publicly/in front) + SCRIBE (write) = to publicly write against = to FORBID, OUTLAW, BAN. 'The government proscribed the extremist organisation.' PRESCRIBE vs PROSCRIBE: prescribe = recommend/specify; proscribe = forbid/ban. These two are the most commonly confused antonyms in vocabulary sections. PYQ: prescribe vs proscribe distinction in IBPS PO vocabulary.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best fills the blank: The ancient ______ on the temple wall, written in Brahmi script, revealed the king's lineage.

options.option_text: Inscription — IN + SCRIPT = writing carved or engraved on a surface (stone, metal, wall)
Prescription — a prescription is a medical/legal order, not a carved historical text
Subscription — a subscription is an agreement to receive something periodically
Conscription — conscription refers to compulsory military service, not a written historical text

questions.explanation: INSCRIPTION: IN (on/into) + SCRIPT (written) = text carved or written on a durable surface (stone, metal, clay). EPIGRAPHY: the study of inscriptions. EXAMPLES: Ashokan inscriptions (rock edicts/pillar edicts), Indus Valley seals, Ajanta paintings captions, Mahabalipuram inscriptions. CONTEXT CLUES: 'temple wall,' 'ancient,' 'carved' (implied by wall writing) → inscription. DISTINCTION: inscriptions are permanent, carved; manuscripts are portable handwritten documents; prescriptions are medical orders. PYQ: inscription in historical context appears in IBPS PO GA and history questions.

questions.stem: The word CONSCRIPT is related to the SCRIPT root. In the context of military history, to conscript means:

options.option_text: To compulsorily enlist people into the military service (draft) — CON + SCRIPT = to write (enlist) together into service
To write a military strategy document — a strategy document would be a plan or order, not a conscript
To voluntarily sign up for military service — conscription implies compulsion, not voluntary enlistment
To discharge or release a soldier from active duty service (not this) instead however alone too

questions.explanation: CONSCRIPT: CON (together) + SCRIPT (write/enlist) = write people together into a list = draft/compulsory enlistment. NOUN: a conscript = a person who has been drafted. CONSCRIPTION: the system of mandatory military service. INDIA CONTEXT: India does not have conscription currently — military service is voluntary. EXAMPLES: UK conscription in WWI/WWII; US draft in Vietnam War; Israel, South Korea still have conscription. CONTRAST: ENLIST (voluntary) vs CONSCRIPT (compulsory). SUBSCRIBE (sub+scribe): to write one's name under = to agree to receive (magazine subscription) or to support an idea. PYQ: conscript/conscription meaning in vocabulary or current affairs sections.

questions.stem: The authorities decided to ______ the publication after it repeatedly violated press regulations.

options.option_text: Proscribe — PRO (publicly/in front) + SCRIBE (write) = to publicly declare something outlawed or banned
Prescribe — prescribe means to recommend or specify; opposite of banning a publication
Inscribe — inscribe means to write on a surface; does not mean to ban or restrict
Subscribe — subscribe means to agree to receive; the opposite of what the authorities intended here

questions.explanation: PROSCRIBE: PRO (in front of/publicly) + SCRIBE (write) = to publicly write against = to officially prohibit, ban, or outlaw. 'The government proscribed the organisation for inciting violence.' PROSCRIBED LIST: organisations/publications banned by the government. PROSCRIPTION: the act or state of being proscribed. HISTORICAL: Roman proscription = public posting of names of people who were declared outlaws and could be killed. PRESCRIBE vs PROSCRIBE MEMORY TRICK: PreSCRIBE = reSCRIBe = positive (recommend); ProSCRIBE = prOhibit = negative (ban). PYQ: proscribe in vocabulary-in-context questions in IBPS PO/SBI PO English.

questions.stem: Which of the following pairs BOTH derive from the SCRIB/SCRIPT root with the core meaning 'write'?

options.option_text: Scripture and transcribe — SCRIPTURE (holy writings) and TRANSCRIBE (write across/copy) both from SCRIPTUM/SCRIBERE
Scrawl and scroll — scrawl from Old English/Norse; scroll from Old French; neither directly from Latin SCRIBERE
Scalpel andescript — scalpel from SCALPELLUM (to carve/cut); script is SCRIPT but scalpel is not
Scribe and scrub — scrub is from Low German/Dutch (to rub); only scribe is from SCRIBERE (not this)

questions.explanation: SCRIPTURE: SCRIPT (written) + URE (noun suffix) = the writings = sacred texts. Hindu, Christian, Islamic scriptures are all 'the writings.' TRANSCRIBE: TRANS (across) + SCRIBE (write) = to write across = to copy, transfer written content. Used for transcribing audio → text, music scores, legal proceedings. SCRAWL: from Germanic roots (to scratch/crawl) — not Latin SCRIBERE. SCROLL: from Old French 'escroe' — a roll of parchment — not directly from SCRIBERE. SCALPEL: from SCALPELLUM (to scrape/carve) — surgical instrument root is different from writing root. EXAM SKILL: similar-looking words often have different etymological roots.

questions.stem: A 'nondescript' person or object is one that is difficult to describe because they are:

options.option_text: Ordinary and unremarkable — nondescript = having no distinctive features worth describing
Extremely unusual or striking — that would be 'distinctive,' the opposite of nondescript
Impossible to see or invisible — nondescript relates to describing, not visibility
Legally prohibited from being described publicly — that applies to proscribed/classified items

questions.explanation: NONDESCRIPT: NON (not) + DE + SCRIPT (written/described) = cannot be described = lacking distinctive features. 'A nondescript man in a grey coat walked past' — so ordinary that there is nothing memorable to describe. USAGE: often used to describe forgettable, bland, unremarkable things or people — nondescript building, nondescript appearance. ETYMOLOGY INSIGHT: DE + SCRIBE = to write down (describe) the features of something. NON + DESCRIBE = something with no notable features to write down. PYQ: nondescript in RC passages or synonym/antonym vocabulary questions in IBPS PO/SBI PO English.

questions.stem: In a formal letter, 'P.S.' stands for 'postscript.' Given that POST means 'after' and SCRIPT means 'written,' which of the following correctly describes a postscript?

options.option_text: A note appended after the main body of a letter is signed
The formal opening salutation before the body of the letter
A summary sentence placed at the centre of the letter text
The closing paragraph that comes just before the signature line

questions.explanation: POST (after) + SCRIPT (written) = something written after the letter is complete. A postscript is added once the letter is already signed. Option D is a common trap because it also appears near the bottom, but a closing paragraph precedes the signature whereas a postscript follows it.

questions.stem: An academic 'transcript' is an official record of a student's grades and courses. Which word-breakdown most accurately captures the etymology and meaning of TRANSCRIPT?

options.option_text: TRANS (across/over) + SCRIPT (written) = a written copy or record
TRANS (beyond) + SCRIPT (speak) = an extended spoken verbal account
TRANS (change) + SCRIPT (seal) = a certified and officially stamped file
TRANS (true) + SCRIPT (data) = a digitally verified academic database

questions.explanation: TRANSCRIPT = TRANS (across) + SCRIBERE (to write); it literally means a 'written-over' copy — hence an official written record. Options B–D incorrectly redefine SCRIPT as 'speak,' 'seal,' or 'data,' none of which reflect the Latin root scribere.

questions.stem: The verb CIRCUMSCRIBE comes from CIRCUM (around) + SCRIBERE (to draw/write). When a constitutional amendment 'circumscribes' the executive's powers, the amendment most precisely?

options.option_text: Broadly extends the executive's reach across all governing domains
Formally publishes the executive's powers in an official public gazette
Draws a boundary around those powers, restricting their permissible scope
Transfers written authority from the executive over to the legislature

questions.explanation: CIRCUM (around) + SCRIBERE (draw/write) = to draw a circle around, hence to set firm limits or boundaries. Option B is a common trap because 'formally publishes' sounds writing-related, but circumscribe means to bound or restrict, not merely to document.

questions.stem: A historian 'ascribes' the invention of the decimal system to ancient Indian mathematicians. The word ASCRIBE (from AD + SCRIBERE) most precisely means?

options.option_text: To engrave a commemorative inscription on a prominent historical site
To formally attribute or credit something to a particular source
To compile an exhaustive written bibliography listing all source texts
To copy a manuscript verbatim as found in the original archive

questions.explanation: ASCRIBE = AD (to) + SCRIBERE (write) → to assign or write something to a cause or person, i.e., to attribute credit. Option D is the key distractor — it confuses ascribe with transcribe; Option A conflates the figurative act of ascription with the physical act of engraving.

questions.stem: In the chemical formula H₂O, the numeral '2' appears in 'subscript' (SUB = below). Which SCRIPT-root word correctly names a character written above the baseline, as in the exponent of x³?

options.option_text: Superscript — SUPER means 'above,' placing characters above the line
Overscript — OVER denotes elevation of a numeral above the text row
Exscript — EX signals text that is placed outside the main baseline
Hyperscript — HYPER refers to any numeral raised above standard text

questions.explanation: SUPERSCRIPT = SUPER (above) + SCRIPT (written); it is the standard typographic and mathematical term for characters raised above the baseline. 'Overscript,' 'Exscript,' and 'Hyperscript' are invented terms with no standing in standard usage, though they sound plausible.

questions.stem: Herman Melville's 'Bartleby, the Scrivener' depicts a Wall Street copyist. The word SCRIVENER derives from Old French 'escrivein' (Latin: scribere). Which description best matches the historical occupation of a scrivener?

options.option_text: A licensed pleader who argued civil disputes before colonial courts
A professional copyist who transcribed legal and commercial documents
A royal herald who read imperial proclamations aloud in public markets
A cartographer employed to draft official boundary and survey maps

questions.explanation: A scrivener was a professional writer who copied legal documents, drew up contracts, and acted as a notary before printing became widespread — the SCRIB root (to write) is central to the role. Option A confuses the role with a barrister; Option C describes a town crier or herald, neither of whom is principally a writer.

questions.stem: In Roman imperial law and Catholic canon law, a 'rescript' (RE + SCRIPT) was a specific authoritative document. Which option most accurately defines a rescript in its classical legal and canonical sense?

options.option_text: A written reply by an emperor or pope responding to a legal petition
A revised draft of earlier legislation returned for further amendment
A public notice ordering all citizens to re-register their land titles
A sealed warrant authorising officers to search private written records

questions.explanation: RESCRIPT = RE (back) + SCRIPT (written); in Roman law and Catholic canon law it was the official written response sent back by the emperor or pope to a specific petition or legal inquiry. Option B is the key distractor — it describes a legislative amendment (a revision), not a personal authoritative reply, and conflates RE (back) with RE (again/revise).
